name: The History of Tarot
description: Tarot is in the middle of a 21st-century revival — and to understand why, this course traces the recursion back. A game first; divination added later; the same pictures remade by people, generation after generation, from a 1440s card table to today.
_built_by: Converted once from course/history-of-tarot.mdx on 2026-10-23; this file is the source now (edit it, or the grammar in recursive.eco).

sections.Content:
> *"There is in fact no history prior to the fourteenth century. The deception and self-deception regarding their origin in Egypt, India or China put a lying spirit into the mouths of the first expositors… The true Tarot is symbolism; it speaks no other language and offers no other signs."*
>
> — **A. E. Waite**, *The Pictorial Key to the Tarot* (1910), Parts I–II — the occultist who directed the design of the Rider-Waite-Smith deck, on the cards' invented past and their real substance

*One note before we take Waite's word for anything.* He is the best primary-source debunker of the Egyptian story we have, and he is not a neutral witness: in the same 1910 book he replaces the false history with a false timelessness — a Secret Doctrine behind the cards "which has always existed", a claim engineered so that no document could ever count against it. Refuting a datable invention and installing an undatable one is not the same as clearing the ground. The cruder version leaves fingerprints; the refined one has learned to wear gloves. Read the epigraph as a good debunk by a man with his own thing to sell.

Tarot is everywhere right now. New decks are crowdfunded by the thousand; readings fill the social feeds; the cards thread through fashion, music, and therapy. A four-suit card game has become, in the 2020s, a genuine cultural force — the survey data and search trends are laid out in [Tarot Today](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=tarot-today); here we ask where it actually came from.

Not where its own mythology points. Much of what people are told about the cards — that they descend from ancient Egypt, that they hold a lost hermetic key — was invented late, in 1781. The documentary record is clear: tarot began as a *game*, a luxurious card game played in the courts of northern Italy in the 1440s. The divination, the Egyptian myths, the promise of secret wisdom were all added afterward, by people, layer upon layer — the container came long before the content. What runs unbroken from that first card table to a phone screen today is not a hidden ancient truth but a recursion: the same pictures, their meaning made and remade, generation after generation. That recursive history is the subject here.

That is what makes tarot worth our attention here at [recursive.eco](https://recursive.eco), which is really a place about one thing: how human beings make meaning *together*, and hand it on, and remake it. The cards are a near-perfect specimen of that process. Because the divination was *added* rather than revealed, it never carried any binding authority — there is no pope of tarot, no scripture, no one who can tell you that you have read a card wrongly. That openness is the whole point. Anyone who picks up the cards becomes, in a small way, an author of meaning.

It is also why the cards can serve us now. There is an arch in how *these* cards have been held — **game → crystal ball → gate** — and it is a history, not a law. This deck's meanings hardened on particular dates and in particular hands: 1781, when Court de Gébelin declared the trumps Egyptian; the 1780s and 90s, when Etteilla built decks to sell fortunes from them; the nineteenth-century drawing-room and fairground trade that made the crystal ball the picture everyone still has of a card reader. But a game is a safe container, and inside it a card stops being an oracle and becomes a **gate, not a fate**: it asks what is already alive in you rather than dictating what is to come. This is the same move a narrative therapist calls *externalising* — the problem is the problem, the person is not the problem — and the same instinct that puts a crayon in a hand in art therapy. It is why the Tower can be read as a lesson in radical acceptance instead of a prophecy of ruin. Knowing that a game sits underneath it all is precisely what loosens meaning's grip, and lets us put these old pictures to more adaptive use.

There is another way the cards become a gate. Held forward instead of back, a spread is a way to *imagine* a possible future — and a future we can picture, we are likelier to make. That is the self-fulfilling edge of reading: a generous view, practised, tends to come true, the way a hopeful account of a relationship can help bring the relationship about. So the responsibility is ours — to be careful which prophecies we choose to make real. How humans have used lots, oracles, and signs to choose well is its own long story, told in [the divination traditions](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=divination-traditions).

So we begin where the cards themselves began — with the journey west — and only then turn to the question every reader brings to them: whether, at bottom, any of it is magic.

nodes.name: Before Tarot — the cards come west

sections.Content:
Long before the first tarot was painted, the cards themselves had already travelled half the world. Most scholars trace them to **Tang or Song China** — perhaps by the ninth or tenth century — as "money-suited" cards, an echo of which may survive in the Chinese [Mǎ Diào](https://recursive.eco/play?id=51858640-0605-4428-b6b0-633b115f642e) (馬吊) games; the earliest stages are thinly documented and still debated. From there they moved westward along the trade routes of the Islamic world. The [Mamluk cards](https://recursive.eco/play?id=2403af8b-1350-4df4-b04c-976ebe5c9326) of Egypt and Syria — an incomplete pack of which survives in Istanbul's Topkapı palace — carried four suits: cups, coins, swords, and polo-sticks.

Watch those four suits, because they are about to become something familiar. Cups, coins, swords, and polo-sticks become the European **cups, coins, swords, and batons** — the very suits still shuffled today. India's [Ganjifa](https://recursive.eco/play?id=aacf7645-23da-442b-9125-29c4ca7ce91d) is a cousin from the same broad family.

When these cards reached Europe, in the 1370s, they arrived not as an idea but as a finished thing: a complete four-suit game that had already crossed deserts and seas and passed between several card-playing worlds. The Italians, about seventy years later, added a novelty of their own — a second, higher set of cards laid *over* the four suits, like a new layer of life settling over an older one. Those are the **trumps**, and they are a good piece of game design, in the same register as the inventions that preceded them. Everything else, the suits you hold in your hand, was made in China, remade in Mamluk Egypt and Syria, and has cousins in the Ganjifa packs of India — three distinct traditions, not one compass direction.

nodes.name: The First Deck — and What Came Before

sections.Content:
The trump idea had a prelude. After the Black Plague, the Roman demagogue **Cola di Rienzo** revived antiquity's **triumphal processions** as civic spectacle, and his friend **Petrarch** turned them inward in *I Trionfi* — a sequence of allegorical figures each conquering the last: Love overcome by Chastity, then Death, then Fame, then Time, then Eternity. That *ordered procession of pictures, each triumphing over the one before,* is the mould the trumps were cast in.

The very first deck of this kind is lost — but its text survives. Around 1418–1425, **Marziano da Tortona**, secretary to Duke Filippo Maria Visconti of Milan, wrote out a game of **sixteen Greek gods** played over **four "bird" suits** (eagles, phoenixes, turtledoves, doves), its cards painted by Michelino da Besozzo. The cards vanished; the treatise endured only because **Jacopo Antonio Marcello** mailed it to Isabella of Lorraine in **1449** — by then already out of date, since Milan had moved on to the newer 22-trump decks. It was not yet a tarot (sixteen gods, not twenty-two trumps), but it is the documented first move. (Full sources, and the honest "reconstruction, not artifact" caveat: the [research dossier](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/decks/marziano-da-tortona.md).)

We have followed the cards west; now watch what people actually *did* with them. The answer, for three centuries, is that they **played**. The game tarot belongs to is the **trick-taking game** — the same broad family as Whist, Bridge and Hearts — in which each player lays a card to the table and the strongest one sweeps the pile. Cards had reached Europe as gambling equipment, and trick-games were the thing they were overwhelmingly used for.

The Italian novelty of the 1440s was a stroke of pure game design: a fifth, permanent suit of pictures that outranked all four ordinary suits at once. They called these cards *trionfi* — triumphs; we call them **trumps**, the word simply *triumph* worn smooth — and that single idea proved so useful it spread out of this game into countless later ones. So tarot did not merely *descend* from card games; it handed them one of their most enduring mechanics. Every time you "trump" a trick in any modern game, you are echoing the Italian *trionfi*.

The game itself travelled and split into regional dialects, each on its own pack: the swift **Tarocchino** of Bologna on a shortened 62-card deck, the vast **Minchiate** of Florence on ninety-seven, the French Tarot still dealt in cafés today. The rules drift; the core holds — follow the led suit if you can, and when you cannot, a trump triumphs. And you can still play it: we have built two of these to try in your browser from the open decks in this library — the authentic four-handed **[Tarocchino di Bologna](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/games/tarocchino.html)**, and a gentler one-on-one introduction, **[Trionfi](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/games/trionfi.html)** (the whole shelf is on the **[Play](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/play.html)** page). The family even reaches back past tarot itself: the **Mamluk** game that first carried the four suits into Europe is *lost* — no rules for it survive — but its Chinese ancestor, the money-suited **[Ma Diao](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/games/madiao.html)**, was written down in Ming-dynasty manuals, so one of the oldest card games whose rules survive is playable here too. Knowing the cards as a game first is the surest way to feel how much meaning was *added* afterward. (For how the games were actually scored and played, see John McLeod's [rules at pagat.com](https://www.pagat.com/tarot/ottocento.html) and the deck's [research dossier](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/decks/tarocchino-bologna.md).)

No tradition this old ever travels in a straight line. Observe tarot across the centuries and you see something that behaves less like an invention and more like a living lineage — spreading, dividing into families, hybridising with its neighbours, and yet remaining recognisably itself the whole way through. From its roots in Italy — the gold-ground [Visconti-Sforza](https://recursive.eco/play?id=6dc092b0-9972-43f0-b493-ff6c2a61dcfc) cards painted for a Milanese duke — it branched south into Florence and Bologna, east into Ferrara, west toward the workshops of Marseille whose [Conver deck](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ac47f7af-ac80-4942-a422-dd4a15614738) fixed the standard pattern, and at last into the hands of the occultists — from [Court de Gébelin](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ba98bf95-e08d-409f-a16c-2dcb660e4545) to the [Golden Dawn](https://recursive.eco/play?id=edac5d5a-8100-486d-b822-2f31b20a194c) — who would redraw it entirely.

![The Lineage of Tarot](https://tarot.recursive.eco/print/book/figures/lineage.png)

*The Lineage of Tarot. [Open the live family tree](https://tarot.recursive.eco/viewers/genealogy-tree.html), where every deck opens.*

![Timeline, 1440s to 1900s](https://tarot.recursive.eco/print/book/figures/timeline.png)

*Timeline, 1440s to 1900s. [Open the live timeline](https://tarot.recursive.eco/viewers/timeline.html).*

nodes.name: The three Ways — how the family split

sections.Content:
After the Milanese **Roots**, the game travelled, and as it travelled the *order of the trumps* drifted from city to city. Sorting the surviving evidence, the historian **Michael Dummett** found the twenty-two trumps had been numbered in three distinct regional patterns — he labelled them, without ceremony, **A, B, and C**. Those three orders are the three "Ways" branching across the [Tree of Tarot](https://tarot.recursive.eco/viewers/genealogy-tree.html):

- **The Southern Way · Order A · Bologna & Florence** — home of the swift [Tarocchino](https://recursive.eco/play?id=37ff6a9d-ba38-42e2-92ea-aa5871716bcc) and the vast ninety-seven-card [Minchiate](https://recursive.eco/play?id=2fd5ebb0-a69d-4731-9acd-bbf4e37c17e8).
- **The Eastern Way · Order B · Ferrara** — the court of the d'Este; the so-called ['Charles VI'](https://recursive.eco/play?id=cc5bda4c-f47b-43e9-aa35-d3164f7c3c0e) cards.
- **The Western Way · Order C · Milan, carried west** — into Savoy and France, where the [Tarot de Marseille](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ac47f7af-ac80-4942-a422-dd4a15614738) (the Conver pattern, the [Besançon](https://recursive.eco/play?id=0aab46a2-38b1-4ba3-8dc1-914af67a026c) variant) fixed the order almost every modern deck still follows.

Here is why that small fact about *numbering* matters so much. The occultists who came later treated the sequence of the trumps as a sacred, fixed key — a hidden alphabet whose order *meant* something eternal. But the order was never fixed. Three cities kept three different sequences, disagreeing mostly about where to slot the three Virtues. A thing that varies by town is a game design, not a revealed cosmology. The regional drift of the trump order is the single cleanest piece of evidence that tarot was a game that *acquired* meaning — never a book of secrets that always had it.

Two branches grow off to the side of the main trunk:

- **The Occult Reframing** (France → England, from 1781): [Court de Gébelin](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ba98bf95-e08d-409f-a16c-2dcb660e4545)'s invented Egypt, [Etteilla](https://recursive.eco/play?id=50fb5980-5be5-4702-9a4f-858ddd524fe3)'s fortune decks, then Lévi, Papus, the [Golden Dawn](https://recursive.eco/play?id=edac5d5a-8100-486d-b822-2f31b20a194c) and Waite — where the cards were redrawn as a hidden book of the soul. That tradition keeps its own page here, held as *practice*, not history: [The Golden Dawn — the Map and the Walk](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=walking-the-golden-dawn-path).
- **Sui Generis & Relatives** — the strange ones not quite in the line: the [Sola Busca](https://recursive.eco/play?id=277953bc-b745-419a-a265-484865e75516), the [Mantegna 'Tarocchi'](https://recursive.eco/play?id=44c379aa-5bfa-40d4-91ea-b593e18cbc2d) (not a tarot at all, but an engraved encyclopaedia of the cosmos), and the modern descendants.

And behind all of them, the **Ancestors** — the money-suited [Ma Diao](https://recursive.eco/play?id=51858640-0605-4428-b6b0-633b115f642e), the [Mamluk](https://recursive.eco/play?id=2403af8b-1350-4df4-b04c-976ebe5c9326) cards, the Indian [Ganjifa](https://recursive.eco/play?id=aacf7645-23da-442b-9125-29c4ca7ce91d) — the pre-tarot packs the four suits first rode in on.

We catalogue all this as a **tree** — a genealogy of descent — because that is how the cards actually behave: a single Milanese root, branches into regional families, hybrids where two branches touch, and an unbroken recognisability the whole way down. A tree shows what an alphabetical list cannot — that the Marseille and the Minchiate are *cousins*, that the occult decks are a graft onto an old trunk, that no deck is the "original" and none the "true" one.

One thing to keep straight, because the words collide. Our **Tree of Tarot** is a *family tree* — who descends from whom, an account of history. The esoteric **Tree of Life** that the Golden Dawn later mapped onto the cards is a different tree entirely — a diagram of the soul, not of the past. The first is evidence; the second is practice. We keep them apart — and you can [walk the second one](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=walking-the-golden-dawn-path) if you like.

The tree is only one cut through the cards; there are many, and they are worth playing with. The [Emergence Explorer](https://tarot.recursive.eco/viewers/explorer.html) lets you pivot the whole library by any dimension and watch the patterns surface — *every grouping is an emergence.* Group by **century** and the game's spread across Europe appears; by **order** (A / B / C) and the three Ways separate themselves cleanly; by **function** — *game · divination · esoteric · origin-myth* — and you watch a plaything be slowly made into an oracle; by **suit**, **arcana**, **number**, or **lineage** and still other families come into view. None of these is the "real" structure underneath the others. Each is one true shape among many — which is, in the end, this whole book's argument about the cards themselves.

Each of these decks is a single specimen: a moment in the lineage, preserved. Some are luxurious one-offs, painted in gold for a single Milanese duke; others were cut in wood and printed by the thousand. Oldest first — and every one has its story, and the hands that made it.

Every deck in the library, oldest first. Each link opens the deck, with its story and the hands that made it:

Before the analysis, a moment simply to look — and one card to watch in particular. Here is **Death** across four and a half centuries: the skeleton holds, from the 1450s to 1909, even as the scene around it is rebuilt every time — a standing archer, then a scythe-mower among severed limbs, then an armoured rider on a pale horse. The picture is a fossil; the meaning is poured in fresh each century. It is much of this book's argument in a single card.

### One card across the centuries — Death

[![Death](https://pub-71ebbc217e6247ecacb85126a6616699.r2.dev/grammar-illustrations/tarot-de-marseille-conver/13%20XIII%20Nicolas%20Conver%20Tarot%201760.jpg)](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ac47f7af-ac80-4942-a422-dd4a15614738)

*Death — Tarot de Marseille (Conver), 1760. Three centuries on, the same skeleton now mows a field of severed body parts with a scythe — and the card is left pointedly untitled.*

[![Death](https://pub-71ebbc217e6247ecacb85126a6616699.r2.dev/grammar-illustrations/golden-dawn-book-t-tarot/RWS_Tarot_13_Death.jpg)](https://recursive.eco/play?id=edac5d5a-8100-486d-b822-2f31b20a194c)

*Death — Rider-Waite-Smith line, 1909. The skeleton survives the whole journey but is restaged once more: an armoured rider on a pale horse beneath a rising sun.*

### Continuity & diversity — a few iconic cards

[![Le Mat](https://pub-71ebbc217e6247ecacb85126a6616699.r2.dev/grammar-illustrations/tarot-de-marseille-conver/LE%20MAT%20Nicolas%20Conver%20Tarot%201760.jpg)](https://recursive.eco/play?id=ac47f7af-ac80-4942-a422-dd4a15614738)

*Le Mat — Marseille (Conver), 1760. The same vagabond and his nipping dog, now in woodcut.*

[![The Fool](https://pub-71ebbc217e6247ecacb85126a6616699.r2.dev/grammar-illustrations/golden-dawn-book-t-tarot/RWS_Tarot_00_Fool.jpg)](https://recursive.eco/play?id=edac5d5a-8100-486d-b822-2f31b20a194c)

*The Fool — Rider-Waite-Smith line, 1909. Still the wanderer, stepping off a cliff into the modern deck.*

[![Mamluk card, 14th–15th c. Egypt/Syria](https://pub-71ebbc217e6247ecacb85126a6616699.r2.dev/grammar-illustrations/mamluk-deck/Mamluk%20playing%20card%207.jpg)](https://recursive.eco/play?id=2403af8b-1350-4df4-b04c-976ebe5c9326)

*Mamluk card, 14th–15th c. Egypt/Syria — the four-suit ancestor that reached Europe in the 1370s.*

The history is on the table; now the question every reader brings to these cards. Was the tarot, in its origins, a thing of magic? The honest answer, the one the evidence gives, is *no*. For its first three centuries the tarot was a game — the point Michael Dummett spent a career establishing — and nothing in the surviving record suggests otherwise. The point of this book is not that the cards were always magical. It is that an ordinary card game was, over time, *made* magical — that meaning was poured into these little pictures until people could read a whole cosmos in them. Here is the case, laid out plainly.

### The documented origin is a game

Tarot appears in 1440s northern Italy (Milan, Ferrara, Bologna) as a trick-taking GAME: 21 'triumph' cards plus the Fool added to an ordinary four-suit deck so trumps beat the suits. The earliest sources are account books, game treatises, tax/guild records and luxury commissions — and the game never died (tarock/tarocchi is still played in continental Europe). For roughly three centuries (c. 1440–1750) there is no surviving evidence that tarot was used for divination; the earliest is a Bolognese sheet of c. 1750 giving meanings for 35 cards [@farley2009, p. 95].

### The concealment hypothesis (stated fairly)

A fair objection: the archive records what was safe to write down. Divination, sortilegio and judicial astrology were spiritually suspect, and the Inquisition prosecuted superstition — so a fortune-teller in 1490 would call it 'just a game,' and any divinatory use of tarot might simply have left no trace. On this view the silence reflects fear, not absence.

### Why it does not hold up

Four problems. (1) TIMING is backwards: tarot appears c. 1440, but the heavy anti-superstition machinery ramps up later (Roman Inquisition 1542, Counter-Reformation) — leaving a century before the crackdown still with no divination evidence. (2) The cards were NOT hidden: they were openly bought, taxed, gifted and played; an underground practice riding the most visible deck in Europe is implausible. (3) Other fortune-telling DID get recorded in the same period — court astrology, and printed lot-books like Lorenzo Spirito's *Libro delle Sorti* (1482); tarot simply isn't part of that documented sortes tradition until the 1700s. (4) The dog that didn't bark: the 15th-c. friar's sermon (*Sermones de ludo cum aliis*) lists the 21 trumps by name and condemns the deck — as gambling and the devil's work, NOT as divination, the graver sin moralists were eager to catalog. And the 18th-c. emergence reads as invention, not inheritance: Court de Gébelin presents the Egyptian 'Book of Thoth' as a fresh discovery (and gets Egypt flatly wrong), while Etteilla carries his card-reading system over to the tarot.

### From game to oracle, step by step

In France the change can be dated almost year by year. 1770: Etteilla's first book tells fortunes with an ordinary piquet pack, the first evidence of cartomancy in France [@farley2009, p. 106]. 1781: Court de Gébelin's *Le Monde primitif*, vol. 8, declares the tarot an Egyptian book, and the Comte de Mellet's essay in the same volume proposes divining with it [@farley2009, pp. 102, 106]. 1782: Etteilla asks the royal censors' leave to print an 'Egyptian' reading of the 78 cards; it is refused, no reason recorded [@farley2009, p. 107]. 1783–85: his four-part tarot book appears, still titled as a way to entertain oneself with the cards [@farley2009, p. 107]. 1788: his own deck [@farley2009, p. 109]. The later Grand Etteilla packs were renumbered for divination alone and could no longer serve the game [@farley2009, p. 111]. Within about eighteen years a card reader with a piquet pack had become the maker of a tarot built for fortunes.

### Conclusion

So the honest claim is not 'only ever a game,' and not 'secretly always divinatory.' It is: tarot was DESIGNED AND FIRST USED AS A GAME; divinatory meaning is a later (18th-century) overlay. Informal cartomancy with cards can't be wholly ruled out and the record is biased — but the Inquisition does not explain the silence, and the simpler reading fits the positive evidence better.

### Sources

Michael Dummett, *The Game of Tarot* (1980); Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis & Michael Dummett, *A Wicked Pack of Cards* (1996); Decker & Dummett, *A History of the Occult Tarot* (2002); Helen Farley, *A Cultural History of Tarot* (2009); Stuart Kaplan, *The Encyclopedia of Tarot*; Andrea Vitali, *Le Tarot* essays (letarot.it); Lothar Teikemeier, trionfi.com. Primary: the *Sermones de ludo cum aliis* ('Steele sermon'); Court de Gébelin, *Le Monde Primitif* vol. VIII (1781, on Gallica/BnF); Lorenzo Spirito, *Libro delle Sorti* (1482).

Court de Gébelin wasn't working alone in spirit, even if he started the fashion. Forty-one years later, an anonymous London hack ran the identical trick on a different set of props: *[The Book of Fate](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/book-of-fate-1822.html)* (1822) sold itself as a translated Egyptian papyrus found in a mummy's tomb and privately consulted by Napoleon — a fabricated pedigree, invented translator included, dressed up exactly the way the tarot's own Egyptian myth was. Different object, same era, same move.

Some of the people who built the modern esoteric decks reached the same verdict from the inside. Robert Wang, who painted the first complete Golden Dawn deck under Israel Regardie, wrote that he had once assumed every occult author was an initiate, and later judged most such books "little more than the blind leading the blind" ([*Expelled from Nursery School*, 2011, p. 19](https://web.archive.org/web/2016/http://robertwangart.com/Expelled%20From%20Nursery%20School.pdf)).

With that settled, we can turn to the deck itself — first its older half, the four suits, and then the twenty-two trumps the Italians laid over them.

Here is the older, quieter half of the deck — and the part that travelled furthest to reach us. In most packs, for centuries, the numbered cards of each suit were purely abstract: four coins, five swords, arranged like wallpaper, meant to be *counted* in a game and nothing more. And then, slowly, something happened to them. Watch a single number — the Five, the Ten — transform from a pattern into a picture, from a quantity into a little scene with a meaning.

One more pattern hides in the suits — in the numbers themselves. For three centuries a Four was simply four coins, a quantity to be counted. Then the occultists gave every number a fixed meaning that holds across all four suits at once, by laying the ten pips over the ten *Sephiroth* of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life. Watch the Five turn sour in every suit and the Six come good in every suit: it is the number speaking now, not the suit. Read straight from the decks' own words, number by number.

And now the trumps themselves — the twenty-two great cards the Italians laid over the suits. Follow any one of them across the decks and you will see the central wonder of this whole story in miniature. The picture holds — the skeleton, the falling tower, the dancing figure — almost unchanged for five hundred years. But the *meaning* poured into that picture is replaced over and over: read first as a piece in a game, then as a moral allegory, then as a key to the cosmos itself.

The remaking did not stop in 1909, or 1781, or the 1440s. The cards are in the middle of another turn of the same wheel right now — crowdfunded by the thousand, carried by queer, feminist, and diasporic communities as a tool of self-authorship, performed on the social feeds, sold as a wellness object and a party game at once. The boom is not a rise in literal belief, which has barely moved; it is a rise in *practice, visibility, and identity use* — people picking up the same old pictures and making them say something new, for communities the old decks never imagined. And here is what most distinguishes this turn of the wheel from the occultists' turn: these decks **sign** their revisions. Motherpeace, Thea's, The Collective Tarot, Slow Holler, Next World Tarot — each says who changed what, and why, on the box and in the book. The older redrawings smuggled theirs in under a curtain and called the result ancient. The latest dialect of the same living language, spoken by people willing to put their names to it.

We opened on the present; we close there too. Why tarot returned, who it is for, and what that tells us about how meaning gets made is its own open question — followed, with the sourced evidence laid out, in **[Tarot Today — a living question](https://tarot.recursive.eco/pages/course-viewer.html?course=tarot-today)**.

*This course is a frame, not a finish.* The Dummett-school record is unusually clean, but it is not closed.
